canonical_statement: The review aimed to identify and assess system-level interventions intended to improve the safety and quality of prescribing inpatient therapeutic anticoagulation, including anticoagulant selection, dosing, and monitoring.
The review protocol was registered in PROSPERO as CRD42017055476.
The review was conducted using PRISMA guidance.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: conducted using the Preferred Reporting Items

canonical_statement: Eligible studies evaluated system-level interventions for initiated or continued oral or parenteral therapeutic anticoagulation for any indication in hospitalized adults aged 18 years or older in economically developed countries with health systems comparable to Australia.

canonical_statement: The review excluded interventions targeting prophylactic anticoagulation, intra-operative anticoagulation, outpatient or transition-to-outpatient care, and comparisons against control practices no longer consistent with current practice.

canonical_statement: Eligible study designs were randomized controlled trials, non-randomized controlled studies, controlled before-after studies, and interrupted time-series studies; uncontrolled and cross-sectional studies, reviews, unpublished studies, opinion pieces, and conference abstracts were excluded.

source_anchor.paragraph: Scope of the review and eligibility criteria

canonical_statement: The authors searched EMBASE, MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, Pretty Darn Quick-Evidence, and Health Systems Evidence from inception through 24 March 2018 without language restriction, and also reviewed references of shortlisted papers and reviews.
Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts and then full texts, with disagreements resolved by discussion and full-text disputes adjudicated by a third reviewer.

Two reviewers independently extracted study design, intervention, patient characteristics, and all safety and quality outcomes relevant to the review question using the EPOC Data Extraction and Assessment Form.
Risk of bias was assessed independently by two reviewers using EPOC criteria, grading each criterion as low, unclear, or high risk, with third-reviewer adjudication of disagreements.

Interventions and sufficiently similar outcomes were pooled using inverse-variance random-effects meta-analysis in RevMan 5.3; heterogeneity was assessed with I-squared and statistical significance was set at two-sided p < 0.05.
Nineteen included trials contributed 12,742 participants; individual study sizes ranged from 30 to 2,117 participants, with a median study size of 148.
All 19 included studies were randomized controlled trials: 13 randomized by patient, 2 by provider, and 4 by ward or hospital.

The authors grouped interventions into five categories: anticoagulation consultation services, decision-supported warfarin dosing, heparin monitoring systems, other clinical decision support systems, and systematic education and feedback programs.
At least one high-risk-of-bias domain was identified in eight included studies, with frequent concerns about randomization procedures, allocation concealment, and outcome assessment.
No included study specifically evaluated interventions to improve prescribing of low-molecular-weight heparins or direct-acting oral anticoagulants.

As reported by the systematic review, a physician-led anticoagulation consultation service in Landefeld et al. was associated with a 58% lower rate of in-hospital bleeding than standard care (95% CI 2% to 82%; p = 0.03).

canonical_statement: Across seven studies of decision-supported warfarin dosing, no individual study demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in safety outcomes.
Meta-analysis of three decision-supported warfarin dosing studies found no significant reduction in major bleeding versus control (odds ratio 0.46, 95% CI 0.10 to 2.09; p = 0.31; I² = 0%).

population.label: Participants in three pooled warfarin decision-support studies

canonical_statement: Meta-analysis of three comparable studies found a higher proportion of time in therapeutic INR range with decision-supported warfarin dosing; the source-oriented pooled mean difference (control minus decision support) was -11.55 percentage points (95% CI -18.21 to -4.89; p = 0.0007; I² = 0%).

canonical_statement: Across the three heparin monitoring-system studies, none demonstrated a statistically significant safety benefit, and all three had high risk of bias.

In Strom et al., a hard-stop electronic alert prevented co-prescription of interacting drugs in 111 of 194 alert episodes (57.2%) versus 20 of 148 (13.5%) with standard care; the review reports an odds ratio of 0.12 (95% CI 0.045 to 0.33).

population.label: Alert episodes reported for the Strom hard-stop process outcome

canonical_statement: In Silbernagel et al., a passive electronic alert improved appropriate anticoagulant selection to 22% versus 15.9% under standard care (p = 0.021).

population.label: Silbernagel et al. participants as reported by the review

canonical_statement: The passive alert evaluated in Strom et al. did not reduce prescription of interacting medications.

Two multi-centre systematic education and feedback programs did not demonstrate improved anticoagulation safety or quality outcomes; one study reported no change in thrombosis, bleeding, or medical error rates, and the other reported no safety outcomes and no between-group quality improvement.
Most included studies were underpowered to evaluate safety outcomes, and many did not evaluate safety as a primary endpoint.
Heterogeneous populations, interventions, outcomes, and comparison groups limited the authors’ ability to collate and compare interventions.
The lack of recent studies, particularly the absence of studies evaluating direct-acting oral anticoagulants, limits applicability to contemporary practice.
Because diverse intervention types may be indexed using varied terminology, the authors acknowledged that relevant studies could have been missed despite broad anticoagulant search terms.
The authors concluded that the evidence base was insufficient in quality and quantity to recommend any reviewed intervention for routine implementation.
The authors considered anticoagulation consultation services, decision-supported warfarin dosing, and possibly electronic prescriber alert systems worthy of further investigation.

The authors recommended that future controlled trials be adequately powered for safety outcomes, target high-risk patients, include standard-care controls, use evidence-based quality markers as safety surrogates, and evaluate interventions for LMWH and DOAC prescribing.
The review states that pharmacogenetic warfarin dosing algorithms cannot be recommended on the basis of the reviewed evidence.
The authors declared that they had no competing interests.
